papers.title: Reply on RC1
papers.summary: Abstract. Tectonic suture zones on the Tibetan Plateau, as structurally weak belts, commonly host numerous large to very large rockslides. However, how the material composition and structural architecture of suture zones govern the initiation and evolution of landslides remains poorly understood. This study focuses on the Jinsha River suture zone (JSSZ). Through systematic field geological investigations, laboratory microstructural analyses, and landslide inventory statistics, we elucidate the control of tectonic mélange belt lithology and structure on landslide development, and construct a four-stage dynamic conceptual model from initiation to triggering. The results indicate that the heterogeneous, weak lithologies and complex structures of the suture zone provide the fundamental material and structural basis for landslide initiation. Sliding surfaces are not randomly distributed but predominantly localized along sub-horizontal foliation planes or lithological interfaces. These pre-existing discontinuities, under tectonic uplift and river incision, become preferential pathways for stress release and progressive weakening, resulting in clustered landslide distribution along the suture zone. Accordingly, a four-stage initiation and evolution model is proposed, systematically explaining the complete dynamic process from suture zone formation establishing the material-structural framework, through tectonic uplift and river incision driving rock mass fracturing, freeze–thaw cycles and chemical weathering causing progressive coalescence of the sliding surface, to final triggering of catastrophic failure. This study reveals the fundamental control of suture zone lithology and structure on landslide initiation, shifting the analytical perspective from short-term triggers to long-term dynamic coupling, and from external driving conditions to intrinsic lithological-structural constraints. The findings provide a new theoretical framework for understanding clustered rockslide

Community Social Capital and Disaster Resilience in Rural Indonesia: An Integrative Social Science Review
papers.summary: Disaster outcomes in rural Indonesia are shaped not only by the intensity of hazards but also by the social relationships through which communities communicate, cooperate, and access resources. This integrative review examined how community social capital contributes to disaster resilience in rural Indonesia and under what conditions it fails to do so. A purposive corpus of 39 sources (22 peer-reviewed articles, 5 scholarly books or chapters, 3 national regulations, and 9 institutional documents) was identified through 150 database, giving priority to publications from 2016 to 2026 while retaining foundational works. The sources were synthesized thematically using four analytical categories: bonding, bridging, and linking social capital, and participatory knowledge. The synthesis indicated that bonding ties accelerate information sharing, mutual assistance, and psychosocial support in the first hours after a hazard strikes, although most of this evidence comes from outside Indonesia. However, dense internal networks may exclude women, migrants, persons with disabilities, poor households, and other groups with weaker access to community institutions. Bridging and linking relationships are therefore needed to widen participation and to connect villages with government agencies, health services, humanitarian organizations, and technical expertise. Local knowledge was most useful when it was documented and integrated with scientific risk information through participatory planning. Situation reports from the 2025–2026 floods and landslides in Sumatra are consistent with the need for multisectoral coordination and institutional learning. The review proposes a social resilience chain, a conceptual framework not yet tested empirically, that links trust, communication, coordination, collective action, and reflective learning, and concludes that rural resilience is a social process requiring investment in relationships alongside infrastructure and early-warning systems.

Activity and Rainfall Response of the Gimigliano Landslide (Southern Italy): Insights from SBAS-InSAR Data Analysis
papers.summary: Slow-moving landslides are complex systems characterized by marked spatial and temporal variability in deformation, which may be difficult to capture using landslide-wide displacement measures. This study investigates the Gimigliano landslide (Calabria, southern Italy), a large, long-lived and urbanized slope instability, by integrating multi-temporal Sentinel-1 SBAS-InSAR observations, data-driven kinematic segmentation, geomorphological analysis and rainfall–deformation relationships. InSAR time series were clustered to identify spatially coherent kinematic domains, which were subsequently compared with independently mapped geomorphological sectors. Continuous and event-based analyses were then used to investigate the temporal relationship between rainfall and landslide deformation. Four kinematic domains were identified, with the highest domain-averaged deformation rates reaching approximately −12.8 mm/yr in the vertical component and −4.8 mm/yr in the east–west component. The identified domains show a clear spatial correspondence with the geomorphological elements of the landslide. Rainfall–deformation relationships showed the highest-magnitude correlations for 60–120 days rainfall accumulation windows, with maximum correlations occurring at lags of approximately 30–35 days for the vertical component and 60–75 days for the east–west component. Event-based analysis further highlighted variable response magnitudes among domains and delayed responses within a few weeks. The results indicate that deformation is associated with antecedent hydrological conditions while retaining substantial spatial heterogeneity, highlighting the value of integrating InSAR, geomorphological and rainfall information for the interpretation of slow-moving landslide dynamics.

Near-complete 3D deformation mapping from Sentinel-1 through extended burst overlap interferometry
papers.summary: Despite the widespread application of satellite radar interferometry (InSAR) for measuring surface deformation, the inability to retrieve precise three-dimensional (3D) displacement remains the fundamental limitation, restricting our ability to fully characterise Earth dynamics. Here, we present a new way to recover near-complete (∼86%) 3D displacement fields from Sentinel-1. The method exploits burst overlap regions, which we extend across-and along-track, increasing the usable overlap area by 800%. We apply the approach to glacier and earthquake case studies and demonstrate that the north–south component of displacement can be robustly retrieved with a precision of 40 mm, a factorof-10 improvement over the standard approach incorporating radar intensity offset estimation (410 mm). By providing routine retrieval of the full displacement vector from Sentinel-1 InSAR, our approach enables improved quantification of rapid events, such as earthquakes and magmatic intrusions, and longer-term processes, including interseismic strain accumulation, slow-moving landslides and glacier flow.

papers.title: Coseismic rock slope deformation at different failure stages - towards assessing the likelihood of high hazard avalanching failures
papers.summary: Landslide hazard is the probability of occurrence of an event of a given magnitude in a specific area and time period. The failure mechanism of the mass, and displacement needed to transition the hillslope from metastable to failure are fundamental inputs for coseismic landslide hazard analyses. In closely-jointed rock mass, joint-step-path failure mechanisms evolve with increasing rock-mass displacement. Three main stages have been hypothesized; incipient, transitional and avalanching. Investigating and characterizing these failure-stage transitions is critical for quantifying coseismic landslide hazard as the hillslope-specific scale. However, little is known about the magnitudes of rock mass displacement associated with these transitions. This study aims to quantify the hillslope displacement magnitudes required to transition a rock mass to failure. These thresholds are based on remote sensing measurements of displacement and derived estimates of normalised translational slope displacement (TSDs) - used as a proxy for rock mass deformation or strain - for six coseismic landslides situated in closely-jointed greywacke. Our results show that for a rock mass to transition from metastable to failure - the rock avalanche stage - requires TSDs greater than 5%, where the amount of TSD required varies with the hillslope angle. We propose an empirically-derived “translational slope deformation index” (TSDI); a function of the translational angle of displacement and normalised displacement along it. This novel tool could provide the link between the permanent slope displacements estimated using analytical methods, to the likelihood that a slope will transition into a more mobile, hazardous rock avalanche, during earthquake shaking.

papers.title: Landslide Susceptibility Mapping Using RF ‐Reconstructed SBAS ‐ InSAR Deformation and Ensemble Learning in Wanzhou District, Chongqing, China
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Accurate landslide susceptibility assessment in mountainous regions is often constrained by the reliance on static environmental factors and by spatial discontinuities in SBAS‐InSAR‐derived deformation caused by decorrelation. To address this widely encountered problem in vegetated and topographically complex landslide‐prone regions, this study proposes a potentially transferable workflow for static‐deformation‐informed landslide susceptibility assessment that integrates SBAS‐InSAR deformation reconstructed using a standard random forest (RF) regression model with ensemble machine learning. Wanzhou District, Chongqing, China, located within the Three Gorges Reservoir Area, was selected as a representative mountainous study area influenced by reservoir‐related hydrological processes. Mean line‐of‐sight deformation rates were retrieved from ascending Sentinel‐1A SAR images acquired between January 2020 and December 2024. Fifteen static conditioning factors and a historical landslide inventory were compiled, and RF regression was used to reconstruct deformation in low‐coherence areas. The reconstructed deformation field was then incorporated as a multi‐year deformation‐based conditioning factor into landslide susceptibility modelling. Four models, including RF, XGBoost, LightGBM, and Stacking, were developed under static‐only and static‐deformation‐informed scenarios. papers.title: Research Progress and Prospect of Investigation and Monitoring Technology for Coastal Zone Geological Environment
papers.summary: ABSTRACT The coastal zone, as a dynamic interface where the lithosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere and atmosphere interact, represents a vital area for national economic and social development whilst facing escalating geological challenges and disaster risks. This review systematically synthesizes recent technological advancements in geological environment investigation and monitoring within coastal zone. It focuses on innovations in high‐resolution seismic profiling, multi‐beam bathymetry, in situ testing and sensor networks that have significantly enhanced the precision of submarine structural mapping, hazard identification and resource assessment. A major achievement is the establishment of an integrated three‐dimensional (space–air–land–sea–well) observation framework, which synergistically combines satellite remote sensing, unmanned aerial vehicles, survey vessels, seafloor observatories and borehole systems to enable comprehensive spatiotemporal surveillance. This framework has been applied to developing early warning capabilities for typical geohazards, including coastal erosion, seawater intrusion and submarine landslides. The paper also critically examines existing technical bottlenecks, such as data fusion, real‐time transmission and precursor quantification, and projects future directions towards intelligent sensing, process‐oriented mechanistic studies, cross‐platform integration, standardization and international cooperation. Distinct from prior reviews, this work provides a critical assessment of both technological innovations and practical implementations in China's coastal zones, offering a holistic perspective that addresses unresolved challenges and emerging trends, with the ultimate goal of supporting coastal engineering safety, sustainable resource utilization and ecological protection.

papers.title: Post-event information in calendar-year satellite products inflates landslide susceptibility assessments
papers.summary: Annual satellite products, such as the AlphaEarth Foundations and TESSERA embeddings, summarize a calendar year, so the product of a landslide's event year also contains post-event observations. We audited this post-event information in 18 dated events (7 earthquakes, 11 rainstorms; 61,402 landslides), changing only the input year within each event and keeping the points, spatial folds, models and bootstrap clusters fixed. Replacing the prior-year AlphaEarth product with the event-year product raised the out-of-fold AUC by 0.087 (95% CI 0.065–0.110; all 18 events) for a point model and by 0.071 (0.048–0.093) for a patch CNN. The point-model gain was 0.085 after subtracting each event's drift between two pre-event years. On complete maps, the event-year input added on average 0.21–0.22 of the landslide area to the map's top 10% (9 of 9 events; up to 0.46). A training-year × prediction-year decomposition traced the inflation to models that learn the event's surface changes, chiefly its landslide scars; event-year inputs used only at prediction did not inflate within-event scores on average. The inflation grew with the post-event fraction of the year, reaching half its full size when 23–39% of the year followed the event; this relation survived corrections for recovery. TESSERA and plain Sentinel-2 composites behaved alike. In forward tests in three regions, models trained on earlier landslides scored 0.02–0.11 higher AUC on the new event with event-year inputs, whereas legitimate pre-event embeddings helped mainly near earlier landslides. Studies should use only products whose year ends before the event.

papers.title: Same area, different timeframes: unveiling the evolution of landslide patterns and their impact on susceptibility maps
papers.summary: Abstract Landslide susceptibility maps (LSMs) depict the spatial probability of landslide occurrence, typically using data-driven models based on past event distributions. However, these models often overlook temporal changes, assuming that past patterns reliably predict future events. In a rapidly changing world, influenced by factors such as climate change and urbanization, this assumption may lead to inconsistencies in LSMs over time, reducing their predictive accuracy. To investigate this issue, we analyzed a multi-temporal inventory of 1518 landslides over the past 70 years in Wanzhou District, China, a region impacted by significant environmental changes. We first examined the temporal and spatial variations in landslide patterns. Then, we employed random forest (RF) and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) algorithms to create five LSMs, each based on landslide data from different periods. Finally, we conducted a multi-temporal validation to evaluate the effectiveness of these maps in predicting landslides occurring in subsequent decades. Our findings reveal temporal shifts in landslide spatial patterns and changes in the model-derived importance of causal factors. These variations may be associated with changing environmental conditions in the study area. Both RF and XGBoost models produced LSMs with varying patterns depending on the temporal baseline of the landslide data used. Importantly, the accuracy of these maps decreases as the time span of the inventory data increases. Maps based on short-term data showed higher accuracy, but their predictive power declined rapidly over time, suggesting that in the context of significant environmental changes, LSMs need continuous updates and further spatiotemporal analysis to remain effective.

papers.title: From near-miss to collapse: diagnosing temporal governance gaps in landslide-dammed lake risk management
papers.summary: Landslide-dammed lakes are produced by mass-movement processes and may remain apparently stable before rapid breach or collapse. This study examines the Matai’an Creek landslide-dammed lake in eastern Taiwan to diagnose why recognized hazard signals did not translate into timely structural action. This study develops a temporal diagnostic framework that combines documentary process tracing, case-policy evaluation, phase-based coding of 97 disaster risk reduction actions, and an Escalation Index (EI) to evaluate governance depth across four phases: hazard formation, monitoring and coordination, collapse, and post-collapse adjustment. The analysis clarifies the geomorphological setting, data sources, boundary-delineation workflow, and uncertainty limits, while distinguishing documented evidence from interpretive governance inference. Results show that pre-collapse actions were dominated by monitoring and coordination (EI = 1.36–1.61), whereas structural mitigation and trigger-based intervention emerged mainly after collapse (EI = 3.38–3.42). The findings indicate a temporal governance gap between signal recognition and escalation activation, and demonstrate how near-miss periods can be used as policy stress tests for anticipatory landslide-dammed lake risk management. A temporal diagnostic framework links warning signals to governance escalation. Ninety-seven DRR actions are coded by phase and escalation depth. The Escalation Index quantifies the shift from procedural to structural action. Monte Carlo tests confirm a robust pre-/post-collapse escalation contrast. Near-miss periods reveal missed trigger windows for anticipatory governance.

papers.title: Integrating morphometric analysis and AHP–Monte Carlo framework for multi-hazard risk reduction
papers.summary: Frequent floods, droughts, and landslides in the Pampa River basin of Kerala, India, highlight the need for an integrated approach to multi-hazard watershed prioritization. Traditional hazard assessments often focus on individual hazards and provide deterministic prioritization outcomes without explicitly evaluating uncertainty in decision-making. This study prioritizes 31 sub-watersheds of the Pampa River basin according to their relative susceptibility to floods, droughts, and landslides using a morphometric–Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) framework coupled with Monte Carlo-based uncertainty analysis. Fifteen morphometric and hazard-related parameters representing linear, areal, and relief characteristics were derived from a 30 m Digital Elevation Model (DEM) using ArcGIS. AHP was employed to assign criterion weights, while a Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 iterations was conducted to evaluate the robustness of watershed rankings under uncertainty in expert-derived weights. Results indicate that sub-watersheds W10, W14, W7, W4, and W17 consistently ranked among the highest-priority sub-watersheds across the Monte Carlo simulations, demonstrating the robustness of their prioritization under uncertainty in the AHP-derived weights.Validation using observed household-level flood, drought, and landslide damage data showed strong agreement between modeled priorities and recorded impacts, supporting the reliability of the framework. The integration of morphometric analysis, AHP, and Monte Carlo simulation provides a transparent, uncertainty-aware, and transferable framework for multi-hazard watershed prioritization, supporting disaster risk reduction, watershed management, and climate-resilient planning in data-scarce tropical river basins.

papers.title: Deformation and reinforcement of piled bridge foundations on weathered mudstone slopes
papers.summary: Introduction: With the rapid development of China’s highway system, the construction of bridges spanning valleys in mountainous regions has become inevitable. In these areas, the deformation of bridge foundations must be strictly controlled, often through slopes reinforced with anti-slide piles. Materials and methods: Departing from the conventional “landslide–stabilizing pile” paradigm, this study adopts a holistic system perspective by modeling the “bridge pile–anti-sliding pile–weathered mudstone slope” as an integrated finite element method (FEM) framework, with the Qiezang Bridge on the Linxia–Dahejia Expressway as a case study. The horizontal displacement of the bridge foundation and anti-piles serves as the principal optimization target. Results: The installation of the rear-row anti-pile (P1) alone reduced the maximum horizontal displacement of the bridge foundation from 6.67 mm to 5.07 mm, corresponding to a 24.0% decrease. This confirms that a single-row configuration at the rear effectively enhances the deformation resistance of the foundation. By adjusting the location of the front-row anti-pile (P5) under the prevailing geological conditions, an optimal position of p x = 2.0 m was identified in the case of double anti-slide piles reinforcement. Conclusions: Comparative results indicate that the interaction between piles and soil is highly complex, due to the combined effects of lateral parabolic loads from soil thrust, lateral triangular loads from pile deflection, and soil resistance acting on the piles. Given the prevailing geological setting, the lateral displacement of P5 decreased from 51.2 mm to 34.0 mm at a position of p x = 2.0 m, representing a reduction of 17.2 mm (33.6%) and remaining the horizontal displacement of the bridge within the allowable limit. This provides a quantitative basis for reinforcing bridge foundations on weathered mudstone slopes.

papers.title: Predictive modeling using heterogeneous data sources
papers.summary: The increasing availability of heterogeneous data has transformed the scope and capabilities of predictive modeling across scientific, social, and environmental domains. Modern predictive systems no longer rely on a single structured dataset collected under controlled conditions. Instead, relevant information is distributed across multiple modalities, platforms, temporal scales, and relational structures. Social media interactions generate large volumes of unstructured textual and network data that reflect human behavior and collective attention. Environmental monitoring systems produce high-dimensional geospatial and temporal measurements describing weather patterns, soil properties, and ecological conditions. Scientific repositories and digital libraries contain rapidly growing collections of publications, metadata, and domain-specific representations that require automated extraction and organization. These heterogeneous sources provide substantial predictive potential, but they also introduce significant methodological challenges related to data integration, representation learning, scalability, and generalization. Machine learning has emerged as a powerful framework for extracting predictive signals from such complex data environments. However, conventional approaches often assume homogeneous feature spaces, abundant labeled data, and static distributions. These assumptions rarely hold in real-world predictive settings. Data collected from different sources frequently exhibit variations in semantics, structure, quality, and temporal dynamics. Labels are often scarce, incomplete, or expensive to obtain. Moreover, predictive systems deployed in operational settings must generalize across domains, evolving environments, and previously unseen data distributions. This dissertation investigates predictive modeling under heterogeneous data conditions through a collection of studies spanning social media analytics, environmental hazard prediction, graph representation

papers.title: Rainfall threshold-governed landslide susceptibility in the Himalaya
papers.summary: Study Region The Himalayan range. Study Focus This study develops a coupled modeling approach that integrates I–D thresholds and an optimal model to evaluate landslide susceptibility across different rainfall intensities. New Hydrological Insights for the Region The cumulative antecedent rainfall during the 168 h preceding landslide events exhibits a sublinear power-law relationship with landslide frequency in the Himalaya. The 5%–90% threshold curves show a decreasing trend in intensity with increasing duration. Driven by complex orographic precipitation, the overall pattern of landslide susceptibility in the Himalayas is characterized by higher values in the southern regions and lower values in the northern regions, with spatial variations across the eastern, central, and western sectors. Furthermore, coupled modeling demonstrates that regional landslide event is highly sensitive to rainfall at different quantiles. When the threshold rises from 5% to 90%, the area of very low susceptibility decreases by nearly 50%, while the area of very high susceptibility increases markedly to 17.95% at the 90% threshold. By integrating rainfall thresholds with landslide susceptibility models, this study provides critical hydrological insights into how landslides respond to diverse rainfall conditions across complex terrains, offering a robust scientific basis for regional landslide susceptibility assessment under different rainfall scenarios.

papers.summary: Abstract. Regional landslide debris inundation risk assessments are commonly constrained by scenario-based formulations that require explicit enumeration of landslide sources and runout events, limiting scalability and introducing sensitivity to subjective modelling choices. This study presents a process-based framework for regional landslide debris inundation risk assessment that employs a flux-based hazard metric to quantify probability of inundation and mean annual property loss risk. The approach builds on the Landslide Source-to-Inundation Process Model by coupling spatially distributed landslide sediment production with mass-conservative downslope routing, and converting resulting debris flux into probabilistic estimates of building damage. Risk is evaluated as a temporally integrated quantity arising from all feasible landslide sources, volumes, triggers, and return intervals, without reliance on discrete runout scenarios. We apply the method to the ~25,000 km2 West Coast region of New Zealand. Results indicate the aggregate rainfall-induced property loss corresponds to approximately 1.6 equivalent complete residential-building losses per year under present-day conditions. Under the RCP6 2081–2100 climate scenario, rainfall-induced residential APLR increases by approximately 50 %, assuming landslide sediment production increases in proportion to rainfall-induced susceptibility. Uncertainty is quantified through parametric sensitivity analysis, Monte Carlo simulation, and evaluation of topographic resolution effects. Combined uncertainty is estimated at approximately ±1.0 OOM at the 1-sigma-equivalent level for the regional 25 m model; a conservative ±1.25 OOM uncertainty is adopted for interpretation. This reduces substantially when higher-accuracy topography is employed. The framework provides a scalable and transparent basis for regional landslide risk analysis and supports risk-informed planning in landslide-prone regions.

papers.title: Critical slowing down reveals dynamical regimes of slow-moving reservoir landslides: Hidden Markov model evidence
papers.summary: Slow-moving landslides do not respond uniformly to rainfall and reservoir-level fluctuations: the same hydrological trigger can produce markedly different displacement responses depending on when it occurs. Determining whether a landslide is in a dormant or an active dynamical regime may therefore provide information complementary to conventional hydrological-threshold warning systems. This study applies critical slowing down (CSD) indicators to 17 years of monthly GPS displacement data from three slow-moving reservoir landslides in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area (Baishuihe, Bazimen, Shuping), with a two-state Gaussian hidden Markov model (HMM) serving as an independent statistical validation benchmark. Three findings emerge. First, CSD cannot provide statistically significant lead-time warning ahead of individual displacement acceleration events (all 27 permutation tests p > 0.05 ). Second, CSD indicators, and Variance in particular, show consistent discrimination between dormant and active regimes across the three sites, as validated by the HMM (6/9 point-biserial correlations survive Bonferroni correction). Third, Variance significantly outperforms AR1 at Bazimen and Shuping and across the three sites in meta-analysis (Stouffer combined Z = + 5.60 , p < 0.001 ), with the two indicators statistically tied at Baishuihe, a rank order that reverses the consensus of the ecological CSD literature—a reversal that may be related to the heavy-tailed distribution of monthly landslide displacement increments. Together, these findings suggest that CSD indicators carry regime-classification information not recoverable from hydrological variables alone, and contribute a nonlinear-dynamics perspective to the emerging research strand on regime identification in landslide early warning.

papers.summary: Abstract. The Marmara's Sea with its near-field tsunami complications in Europe and the eastern Mediterranean, is paradoxically surrounded by a densely urbanised, infrastructure-rich coastline and positioned above the North Anatolian Fault system with historical earthquake events, submarine slope processes and narrow-basin resonance that impact coastal water levels. This fact motivated the current study presenting a benchmark-consistent GeoClaw modelling roadmap on seven historical Marmara tsunami scenarios selected from 22-event source catalogue with numerical comparison through 20-lane. The lanes represent exclusively, different source-construction, turning strategy, comprising earthquake-only, earthquake-plus-landslide, adaptive sampling, hybrid site-blend, and close-loop correction variants. From the first lane to the final selected best lane of the simulations set, the benchmark error could be reduced from maximum 1.93 m to 0.019 m in MAE (Mean Absolute Error) and 2.26 m to 0.024 m in RMSE (Root Mean Square Error), with all seven events cases remaining below 10 % error and the largest absolute percent error is 2.4 %. papers.title: Landslide susceptibility assessment in the Western Ghats adjoining Idukki township, Kerala, India, using integrated geomorphological and geotechnical parameters with AHP and machine learning
papers.summary: The Idukki district, Kerala, located in the Western Ghats is highly prone to landslides as the highly rugged terrain responds in complex ways during intense rainfall events. Landslide susceptibility of the region is being assessed in this study by applying Random Forest (RF) and Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) by utilising geomorphological and geotechnical parameters. The methodology involves a systematic workflow that includes data preparation, model development, and validation. Results suggest that while 28.43% and 37.78% of the recorded landslides falls well within the high and very high susceptibility zones, respectively in the AHP model, the RF model shows a more balanced distribution with the smallest area under the very low susceptibility class (13.56%; 9.48 km²) and the largest under the medium susceptibility class (24.60%; 17.18 km²). Model validation using AUC, precision, recall, accuracy, and F1-score attribute a high reliability for the RF model in comparison with the AHP model. Although AHP produced comparatively lower validation scores, all metrics exceeded 0.70, indicating good predictive performance. Also, the ROC–AUC values of 0.99 for RF and 0.85 for AHP further demonstrate the superior accuracy and reliability of the RF model for landslide susceptibility mapping. This demonstrates that by integrating the geomorphological and geotechnical factors based on their relative importance, landslide susceptibility maps can effectively capture the complex relationships between conditioning factors and landslide occurrences.

papers.title: Comment on egusphere-2026-4342
papers.summary: Abstract. Geo-hydrological hazards, including floods and landslides, are among the most widespread hazards and a major cause of human loss worldwide. Their impacts are shaped by meteorological forcing and by long-term changes in exposure, vulnerability, and settlement patterns. Yet robust assessments of long-term fatality trends are rare because sufficiently long, accurate, and homogeneous records of damaging events are lacking. A key unresolved question is whether the human toll of geo-hydrological events has changed structurally through time, and which climatic, socio-economic, or policy factors best explain that change. Here we show, using a unique 1950–2024 catalogue of fatal events in Italy, that geo-hydrological risk underwent a marked transition, with fatalities and fatal days declining sharply until about 1970 and then stabilising at much lower levels. This decline was driven mainly by landslides, whereas flood-related losses showed weaker long-term change. The decline was not explained by specific risk policies or management programmes, as most of it preceded their implementation. Instead, precipitation was the main climatic driver of the remaining interannual variability, particularly for floods and days with fatal events. By contrast, population and gross domestic product did not account for the long-term trends once shared temporal changes were considered. Fatal days were less overdispersed and more predictable than fatalities, suggesting that meteorological factors control more directly the occurrence of dangerous conditions than the final death toll. Fatalities, instead, depend strongly on exposure, vulnerability, timing, location, and other event-specific circumstances. Together, these findings indicate that broad socio-economic dynamics can reduce geo-hydrological mortality even as hazardous processes persist, whereas meteo-climatic conditions continue to shape year-to-year risk.

papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract—Himalayan and global alpine fluvial systems are highly susceptible to sudden-onset disasters, specifically Landslide Dam Outburst Floods (LDOFs) and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs). While the spatial vulnerabilities of these systems are widely mapped via remote sensing, their temporal breach patterns remain critically understudied. This paper examines a recurring temporal phenomenon across both high-altitude Nepalese river basins and international alpine corridors over a multi-decade timeline. The data demonstrate that catastrophic containment failures disproportionately breach downstream zones between the hours of 01:30 and 09:15. By identifying the diurnal thermal and hydrostatic mechanisms behind this "dawn cascade," this study proposes a globally applicable framework for community-based early warning protocols.

papers.title: Resilience and Solidarity of the Kemiri Village Community After Natural Disasters from a Sociological Perspective
papers.summary: Flash floods and landslides in Panti Subdistrict, Jember, disrupted settlements and livelihoods in Kemiri Village and surrounding communities. This article examines how residents have sustained collective resilience through social solidarity, community organization, and locally embedded preparedness practices. Employing a qualitative case-study perspective, it develops the source study's accounts of a neighborhood leader, disaster-related community coordination, and local preparedness initiatives through a sociological interpretation informed by Durkheim's mechanical solidarity and contemporary social-capital scholarship. The reported responses include mutual assistance during evacuation, differentiated responsibilities for residents and young people, cooperation in searching for victims, and post-disaster remembrance through annual collective prayers. Continuing initiatives attributed to the local disaster preparedness unit include identifying evacuation routes, monitoring hazard indicators, providing flotation equipment, and supporting environmental rehabilitation. These practices suggest that shared livelihoods, mutual recognition, and collective memory may facilitate timely cooperation, while structured coordination connects interpersonal support with organized risk reduction. The analysis also distinguishes the observed or reported case material from recommendations drawn from the wider literature: local cohesion cannot replace technical hazard assessment, inclusive risk communication, accessible infrastructure, or sustained institutional support. Because the source does not report a complete interview roster, systematic measurements, or outcome comparisons, causal claims and generalization remain limited. The article argues that durable community resilience depends on combining culturally rooted solidarity with inclusive, accountable, and technically informed disaster governance.

papers.title: Safety performance evaluation of a gently dipping bedding slope containing multiple weak interlayers in Southwest China
papers.summary: The failure modes and safety assessment methods of gently dipping bedding slopes containing multiple weak interlayers (GBSWs) are critical issues in engineering construction. In this study, engineering geological investigations and laboratory direct shear tests on undisturbed samples were conducted to elucidate the strength degradation mechanism and the evolution of strength parameters of the weak interlayers, while finite element simulations were employed to investigate the slope failure modes. Based on the laboratory test results and numerical simulations, a back-propagation neural network (BPNN) model was developed to enable rapid assessment of the operational safety of engineering slopes. The results indicate that the shear strength of the weak interlayers decreases significantly with increasing water content, while both cohesion and the internal friction angle exhibit an exponential decay. The bedrock–overburden interface and the weak interlayers within the slope constitute unfavorable interfaces. Following excavation-induced unloading, slope deformation develops preferentially along these interfaces, resulting in an overall stepped sliding–tensile cracking failure mode. Staged excavation, together with the timely implementation of protective measures after excavation, can effectively control the factor of safety ( F s) and the maximum horizontal displacement (| U x| max ) of the slope. Comparative trial calculations showed that the 5–10–2 BPNN architecture exhibited the best performance, yielding the lowest root mean square error (RMSE) and the highest coefficient of determination (R²). For GBSWs, an analytical limit equilibrium method applicable to the engineering feasibility study and preliminary design stages, together with a predictive assessment method based on machine learning for the safe operation stage, was proposed.

papers.summary: ABSTRACT Wenchuan earthquake–induced landslides generated large volumes of sediment that formed lateral sediment deposits in mountainous river channels, significantly altering flow structures and channel evolution. Under such strongly non-uniform flow conditions, accurate estimation of bed shear stress remains challenging. Because bed shear stress is difficult to measure directly in natural rivers, friction velocity is commonly used as an indirect proxy. This study conducted fixed-bed flume experiments with representative riverbank sediment deposits to evaluate six classical friction-velocity estimation methods under uniform-flow conditions and four methods—the Reynolds shear stress (RSS), turbulent kinetic energy (TKE), vertical turbulent kinetic energy (TKE w′), and logarithmic law methods—under sediment-deposit conditions. The results show that estimated friction velocity is more closely associated with turbulence intensity than with longitudinal mean flow velocity. Turbulence-based methods (RSS, TKE, and TKE w′) showed more consistent responses than the logarithmic law method under strongly non-uniform flow conditions, with the TKE method exhibiting the most stable performance across different flow zones. This study clarifies the applicability and limitations of classical friction velocity estimation methods under different degrees of flow non-uniformity, providing guidance for estimating bed shear stress and conducting sediment-transport studies.

A quantitative geophysical–geotechnical framework for slope stability analysis using electrical resistivity tomography
papers.summary: Abstract Slope instability constitutes a major constraint on infrastructure development in geologically complex and rapidly urbanizing regions such as West Java, Indonesia. Reliable slope stability analysis requires spatial characterization of subsurface mechanical parameters, including cohesion, internal friction angle, and bulk density. Conventional geotechnical investigations provide accurate point-scale data but are often constrained by high cost, limited spatial coverage, and logistical challenges. This study presents an integrated geoelectrical–geotechnical framework enabling the quantitative use of electrical resistivity for slope stability assessment. The investigation was conducted in the Padalarang District, West Bandung Regency, an area dominated by volcanic lithologies. Electrical Resistivity Tomography and Vertical Electrical Sounding were integrated with borehole logs, Standard Penetration Test data, and laboratory measurements to derive empirical correlations between resistivity and key geotechnical parameters. The results indicate a very strong correlation between electrical resistivity (ρ) and cohesion (R 2 = 0.8270), a strong correlation with bulk density (ρᵦ) (R 2 = 0.6860), and a weak correlation with internal friction angle (R 2 = 0.1780). The resistivity-derived parameters were incorporated into limit-equilibrium slope stability analysis under the specified groundwater condition. The representative resistivity-derived parameter model produced a Factor of Safety (FoS) of 2.60, while the final spatially integrated slope model yielded a minimum FoS of 1.23. These results demonstrate that electrical resistivity can provide spatially continuous, site-specific geotechnical information for preliminary slope stability assessment when calibrated and constrained by borehole and laboratory data.

papers.summary: Landslide inventory mapping supports emergency response and hazard assessment in mountainous regions. Accurate identification and delineation of individual landslides remain challenging because of scale variation, irregular morphology, and interference from visually similar backgrounds in complex mountainous terrain. To address these challenges, we modified Mask R-CNN’s feature pathway and mask supervision. ResNet50 was replaced with SwinV2-Tiny for hierarchical feature extraction, while the feature pyramid network (FPN) was retained for multi-scale fusion. Spatially adaptive feature modulation (SAFM) was applied after the FPN to adjust spatial responses using local features and broader context. Binary cross-entropy (BCE) and Dice losses were combined to supervise pixel-wise foreground–background discrimination and instance-mask overlap. A curated dataset combining imagery from Bijie, the Diverse Mountainous Landslide Dataset (DMLD), and ScienceDB was used for training, validation, and internal testing. All configurations were evaluated using the Common Objects in Context (COCO) instance-mask protocol. Across three training seeds, SwinV2–FPN–SAFM Mask R-CNN achieved an internal test average precision (AP0.50:0.95) of 0.6158±0.0082 (mean ± sample standard deviation). Its mean mask AP0.50:0.95 exceeded those of ResNet50–FPN Mask R-CNN and Mask2Former–Swin-T by 6.21 and 3.51 percentage points, respectively. It achieved the highest mean mask AP0.50:0.95 among the ten evaluated configurations. The ablations indicated small positive increments in mean mask AP0.50:0.95 with SAFM and BCE–Dice, and their incremental benefits remained uncertain. The higher mean mask AP0.50:0.95 indicates improved overall performance in identifying landslide instances and delineating their extent on the internal test set. Furthermore, incomplete landslide inventories can also hamper landslide susceptibility assessment quality. Due to all these limitations, more robust methods integrated with geomorphologically based terrain segmentation and advanced machine learning methods are required, which will not only determine the landslide probability zones but also help to understand the landslide driving forces and interaction analysis among the geoenvironmental factors controlling landslides. In the present study, we have used slope unit-based landslide susceptibility mapping, using 4830 slope units, 17 conditioning factors and 8373 of the total updated landslide inventories with six models: random forest (RF), a generalized additive model (GAM), Categorical Boosting (CatBoost), Tabular Neural Network (TabNet), Bayesian additive regression trees (BARTs), and a convolutional neural network (CNN). The model hyperparameters were optimized using Bayesian optimization, except for the BART model. Based on the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve AUC value, RF (AUC = 0.848), BART (AUC = 0.847) and CatBoost (AUC = 0.846) achieved the highest predictive performance. Furthermore, SHAP based analysis shows that most of the landslides are controlled by elevation, aspect, slope, distance to faults, NDVI, proximity to roads and drainage networks. papers.title: GeoBASP: Geography-Aware Structured Pruning for Landslide-Scar Segmentation in the Nepal Himalaya

This study proposes Geography-, Boundary-, and Scar-Aware Structured Pruning (GeoBASP) for compact landslide-scar segmentation. These signals are combined across training blocks within the Koshi Basin using robust statistics to guide pruning under measured computational budgets. Experiments used a spatially separated dataset derived from the ICIMOD Koshi Basin 2024 inventory, Sentinel-2 imagery, and terrain slope. papers.title: Review article: Mountain flash floods: from hazard formation to disaster risk reduction pathways
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Abstract. Flash floods in mountainous regions are becoming more frequent and destructive under climate warming, yet cross-regional understanding of their triggering mechanisms, cascading impacts, and governance remains fragmented. This review synthesises 1,967 studies published during 2000–2025 to establish a globally comparable baseline of mountain flash-flood research. By integrating bibliometric and topic analyses with qualitative synthesis, we reveal pronounced geographical and thematic imbalances, with research concentrated in Europe and Asia. At the same time, many high-risk mountain regions in Africa and South America remain overlooked. Across regions, flash-flood initiation and impacts are shown to be strongly state-dependent and coupled, emerging from interactions between storm intensity, duration and spatial concentration, antecedent hydrological conditions, and hillslope-channel connectivity. This coupling helps explain why fixed rainfall thresholds are difficult to generalise and highlights the need for dynamic, multi-source early-warning approaches. Comparing evidence on early warning, structural protection, and Nature-Based Solutions, the review shows that cascading processes dominate risk management challenges. We therefore propose an adaptive governance framework that links monitoring and forecasting, spatial planning, grey-green integration, and basin-scale risk sharing under non-stationary climate conditions. Overall, this synthesis consolidates fragmented evidence into a cross-regional knowledge base to support flash-flood risk reduction in mountainous regions, where data and capacity are limited.

The water content ranged from 6.6% to 21.0%, the dry density ranged from 1.24 to 1.47 g/cm³, and the applied vertical pressure ranged from 50 to 2000 kPa. The relationships of the collapse coefficient with water content, degree of saturation, dry density, and applied vertical pressure were first examined. Dry density was converted to void ratio, while degree of saturation was calculated from water content and void ratio. Based on the observed nonlinear pressure response, a pressure-dependent formulation with fixed exponents m = 1.6 and n = 1.0 was adopted. The model parameters were further expressed as continuous functions of degree of saturation and void ratio, yielding a three-factor coupled model governed by dimensionless pressure, degree of saturation, and void ratio. Model performance was evaluated using all valid test data and by comparing calculated response surfaces with measured results under different void-ratio conditions. The collapse coefficient generally decreased with increasing water content and degree of saturation, while the influence of pore-structure state depended on both moisture state and applied vertical pressure. The pressure-dependent response was distinctly nonlinear, typically increasing to a peak and then decreasing or approaching a relatively stable value. papers.summary: Abstract Slope instability induced by rainfall infiltration and other sources of water leakage (e.g., pipeline leakage) is a major geotechnical concern, particularly in unsaturated soils, where changes in matric suction can significantly affect the shear strength and stability of the soil slope. This study investigates the hydro-mechanical response of unsaturated slopes subjected to continuous infiltration and evaluates the effectiveness of micropiles in mitigating wetting-induced failures. A two-dimensional finite element model was developed in PLAXIS 2D (V2024.1) using fully coupled flow–deformation analysis. Unsaturated soil behaviour was represented using the soil-water characteristic curve and hydraulic conductivity functions based on the van-Genuchten formulation. The numerical model was validated using field observations from the South-to-North Water transfer Project in Hubei Province, China, and later published numerical studies. Subsequently, the validated model was employed to investigate the performance of micropile-reinforced slopes under infiltration conditions. The study has shown that, under continuous infiltration, the factor of safety (FoS) of the unreinforced slope decreased significantly within 30 days, approaching imminent failure due to the loss of matric suction and a reduction in effective stress. A comprehensive parametric study was conducted to evaluate the influence of micropile position, length, inclination, and diameter on slope performance. The results demonstrated that micropile reinforcement significantly enhanced slope stability, increasing the FoS by about 20% if the most favourable pile-length configuration was adopted. papers.title: Co-producing just sustainabilities: integrating local knowledge and geospatial analysis for climate-sensitive rural settlement planning in the East African Highlands
papers.summary: Highland rural settlements face increasing climate-related hazards, but vulnerability is shaped not only by environmental exposure but also by livelihood dependence, place-based relationships, and governance arrangements. This study examines how local knowledge and geospatial analysis can be integrated to understand rural settlement vulnerability in Rwanda’s Western Highlands. Using a concurrent mixed-methods design, we combined household surveys (n = 280), qualitative inquiry (104 participants), and GIS-based hazard assessment. Results show that landslides, floods, and soil erosion substantially affect rural livelihoods, while perceived risks correspond with spatial patterns of hazard exposure. However, continued residence in exposed areas reflects constrained adaptation choices shaped by agricultural dependence, cultural attachment, institutional arrangements, and limited relocation alternatives. The findings demonstrate that knowledge co-production can provide a basis for socially grounded climate-sensitive planning by connecting spatial evidence with community experiences and addressing questions of risk distribution, knowledge recognition, and decision-making authority.

papers.title: Navigating the Legal Architecture of AI
papers.summary: A state that ignores a 95.6% accurate landslide prediction and then invokes force majeure is not applying a legal doctrine it is abusing one. Force majeure and the Act of God defence share a single operative requirement. Machine learning has destroyed that requirement. AUC values for flood and landslide prediction routinely exceed 0.90 rendering catastrophic events institutionally foreseeable before they occur. The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) reframes the analysis. Classifying disaster-management systems as high-risk AI raises the standard of care for public authorities and makes force majeure progressively harder to sustain as a complete defence. Explainability is a due-process obligation here, not a technical amenity: communities subject to AI-driven evacuation orders hold a legitimate interest in understanding the basis for those decisions. The concern that strict liability will deter disaster-AI deployment is real and deserves a substantive answer. This chapter proposed a standards of domestic enforcement, pre-deployment sandboxes, safe harbours, and compensation funds.

papers.summary: Abstract. We present a methodology to retrieve 3D surface displacement based on Digital Image Correlation (DIC) applied to multitemporal terrain models. Our approach has been developed to overcome the DIC limitation in the vertical component of the displacement field when horizontal shifts are larger than the grid sampling. To validate the performance, we applied the approach to two terrain models acquired over the Brienz/Brinzauls landslide, where surface displacements affect the entire slope with heterogeneous amplitudes and directions. The comparison with in-situ measurements shows that DIC can accurately retrieve horizontal and vertical displacements, providing a clear representation of the spatial extent of the mass movement, as well as an accurate distinction of the internal landslide compartments. Our results are in good agreement with those obtained using a state-of-the-art point correlation method, but require less preprocessing and computational effort. Thus, the proposed DIC strategy can be considered as a valid alternative for measuring 3D surface displacements in scenarios where multitemporal terrain models are available.

papers.title: Classification and Remote Sensing Characterization of Large Catastrophic Landslides in the Southeastern Tibetan Plateau, China
papers.summary: Large catastrophic landslides in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau are characterized by huge volumes and complex chains that frequently cause river damming and casualties. Based on field surveys, multi-temporal satellite imagery, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) deformation measurements, and meteorological and seismic records, this study classifies these landslides into three types by their initiation and disaster-chain processes: (1) rock–ice avalanche → debris flow → landslide dam; (2) debris flow → landslide dam; (3) rock avalanche → landslide dam. Representative cases illustrate the material sources, initiation settings, and downstream impacts of each type. The occurrence of such landslides is influenced by the interplay of four groups of factors: fractured rock masses and abundant loose deposits provide the material basis; high mountains and narrow river valleys provide the spatial framework for landslide evolution and promote river blockage; pronounced climatic changes provide the background conditions and may affect slope stability in glaciated areas through glacier retreat; and frequent strong earthquakes can both instantaneously trigger failure and cause cumulative damage that predisposes slopes to subsequent failures. Ongoing climate warming and repeated seismic activity are expected to increase landslide susceptibility, highlighting the urgency of multi-hazard early warning and proactive mitigation. This study supports early warning prioritization and risk governance in high-mountain valleys across the Tibetan Plateau.

papers.title: faDebrisFOAM: debris-flow modeling with coupled terrain evolution in OpenFOAM
papers.summary: Abstract. Debris-flow numerical models are widely used for hazard assessment and engineering design, yet many models still treat bed evolution in a simplified or uncoupled manner. This study presents faDebrisFOAM, an open-source depth-averaged solver developed in OpenFOAM® that couples debris-flow motion, entrainment, deposition, and terrain evolution within a finite-area framework. The model represents the mixture as an equivalent fluid of variable density and incorporates mass exchanges with an erodible bed layer through entrainment and deposition laws. The Terrain Modification Algorithm (TMA), developed in this work, updates the computational grid at each time step, allowing topographic changes to feed back directly into the governing equations and simulated flow dynamics. The model is evaluated through three applications: validation against large-scale US Geological Survey (USGS) flume experiments, testing in an idealized parabolic geometry, and application to the 2015 debris-flow event in the La Mesilla catchment in northern Chile. The solver reproduces the measured evolution of flow thickness in the USGS flume experiments with good agreement. The idealized application demonstrates that terrain evolution is not a passive output but an active control on run-out, velocity, flow depth, and volume redistribution. The La Mesilla case further shows that coupled terrain modification promotes surge self-generation, self-channelization, and channel-plug formation, which are absent or weakened when the TMA is disabled. These results indicate that coupled terrain evolution can modify flow confinement, stress distribution, and preferential routing throughout the simulation. faDebrisFOAM therefore provides an open-source framework for investigating morphodynamic feedbacks in debris-flow propagation.

papers.title: Spatial assessment of landslide susceptibility in Donomulyo based on GIS-MCDA and AHP
papers.source: Journal of Infrastructure Planning and Engineering (JIPE)
papers.summary: Donomulyo Subdistrict in Malang Regency is characterized by complex hill–coastal terrain that is increasingly pressured by tourism development, making it highly prone to landslides. This study assesses landslide susceptibility using a Geographic Information System–based Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (GIS–MCDA) integrated with the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP). Five conditioning factors—slope, rainfall, land cover, soil type, and geology—were analyzed and weighted through pairwise comparison to generate a spatial susceptibility map. The results show that most of Donomulyo lies within moderate susceptibility zones, reflecting widespread geomorphological instability and emphasizing the need for risk-sensitive land-use management. Scientifically, this research demonstrates the applicability of the GIS–AHP framework to an understudied tropical hill–coastal environment, where local-scale integration of terrain, rainfall, and land-use dynamics remains limited in existing literature. The study’s spatial outputs provide quantitative guidance for zoning, slope conservation, and community-based mitigation—actions that directly support SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), SDG 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 15 (Life on Land). By explicitly linking geospatial hazard modelling with sustainable development planning, this research advances the use of spatial analysis as a decision-support tool for disaster risk reduction and resilient regional development in Indonesia.

papers.summary: Abstract The Eastern Himalayas represent one of the world's most ecologically sensitive and dynamically evolving mountain systems, rendering them exceptionally vulnerable to contemporary climatic shifts. This study presents a comprehensive geospatial assessment of climate-induced hazards in the Papum Pare district of Arunachal Pradesh, India. Situated within the Sub-Himalayan and Lesser Himalayan zones, Papum Pare experiences extreme topographical variance, fragile geological formations and intensive monsoon regimes, culminating in acute susceptibility to flash floods, landslides and slope instability. Utilizing a multi-criteria evaluation (MCE) framework integrated within a Geographic Information System (GIS) and remote sensing environment, this research maps and analyzes hazard susceptibility across the district. Spatial parameters—including elevation, slope angle, slope aspect, lithology, soil characteristics, land use and land cover (LULC), normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and proximity to drainage networks and road corridors—were parameterized, weighted using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) and aggregated to generate district-wide hazard susceptibility indices. The empirical findings reveal that approximately 28% of the geographical area in Papum Pare falls under "High" to "Very High" hazard susceptibility categories, with urbanized expansion zones along river valleys and unengineered infrastructural arteries exhibiting the greatest risk profiles. The results underscore the imperative for localized climate adaptation strategies, risk-informed spatial planning and resilient infrastructure development in the Eastern Himalayan fringe. papers.title: Lithostratigraphically-constrained landslide susceptibility modeling in red-bed basins using a bayesian probability-based mixture probabilistic neural network
papers.summary: Regional landslide susceptibility prediction commonly treats diverse failure mechanisms as a single statistical entity, an oversimplification that fails in lithologically complex red-bed basins, where retrogressive and translational landslides follow fundamentally distinct hydromechanical laws. Here we develop a mechanism-divergent framework that integrates frequency ratio factor screening, Bayesian probability for uncertainty-aware dataset construction, and a mixture probabilistic neural network to explicitly fuse multi-modal susceptibility indices. The approach is validated in Sanshui District, a subtropical red-bed basin in China, using a 15-year multi-source inventory. Random forest and logistic regression are coupled with frequency ratio and Bayesian strategies to independently predict each landslide type. Bayesian-enhanced models consistently outperform their frequency-ratio counterparts, with Bayesian random forest achieving the highest accuracy. The mixture probabilistic neural network captures spatial heterogeneity through distance-weighted neural connections, markedly improving regional mapping and attaining an area under the curve of 90.2%, substantially higher than the 66.7% of conventional unified models. Shapley additive explanation analysis identifies lithology, annual precipitation, and road proximity as dominant controls; lithostratigraphic Groups 1, 7, 12 and 13 exhibit the highest susceptibility. This framework offers a lithostratigraphy-informed, mechanism-aware pathway for landslide risk assessment in complex soft-rock terrains.

V2.9 regression summaries for a 55 mm/h reference run and a no-rain diagnostic were reproduced byte for byte. In the V4.2 reference rerun, the Direct Insertion Method (DIM) and an algebraically equivalent internal-variable update agree to a relative L2 difference of 7.27e-16 in final effective stress sigma_zz. A separate full-history constitutive comparison covers irregular strain increments, holds, and limiting decay factors, with relative L2 differences below 6.72e-16. These results verify the evaluation of the same discrete constitutive history. The package also reports two-level temporal and spatial sensitivity tests and a zero-rain control. Athy–Fernando is deliberately disabled in V4.2 to isolate the viscoelastic contribution; earlier AF experiments are retained as development history. All examples are synthetic. The software is an exploratory research prototype, and operational landslide-warning capability has not been demonstrated. In this work, NP was synthesized via a sonochemical route and its crystallinity was modulated by varying calcination temperatures. At lower calcination temperatures (300–600 ºC), NPs remain predominantly amorphous but turn crystalline when higher temperatures are applied. The thermal treatment also influenced the degree of hydration, particle morphology and pore structure. Among all temperatures, NP calcined at lower temperatures delivered the higher specific capacity and showed predominantly diffusion-influenced Faradaic kinetics. In contrast, NP calcined at higher temperatures showed lower specific capacity, but a stronger surface-control contribution to charge storage. These findings demonstrate that a high degree of crystallinity does not necessarily guarantee high charge-storage capacity and reveal a clear trade-off between active-site utilization and reaction kinetics during the amorphous to crystalline evolution of NP.

papers.summary: Delta-wing flying wings are attractive for small UAVs because they are structurally simple and carry no tail, but the same absence of a tail leaves a single pair of elevons responsible for trim, pitch control and roll control, and it ties static stability to the wing planform. This paper studies how far that single control pair can be sized down before the airframe loses either its stability or its controllability. We build a compact, reproducible model of a 4.5 kg, 1.6 m span delta UAV with a 55° leading-edge sweep: a Helmbold lift slope combined with the Polhamus leading-edge-suction analogy for vortex lift, strip-theory elevon effectiveness, a four-state longitudinal model and a four-state lateral–directional model. Static margin, short-period and phugoid behavior are examined as the centre of gravity moves, and the elevon layout (chord fraction, inboard and outboard station) is then optimized with differential evolution against approach-trim, roll-rate, pitch-authority and hinge-moment requirements. For a 4 % MAC static margin the optimized layout needs 0.083 m² of elevon area, 41 % less than an initial full-span layout, and lowers the hinge moment by 49 %. The study also shows that approach-trim authority, not short-period behavior, caps the usable static margin at roughly 5 % MAC for a section pitching moment of +0.03, and that this ceiling moves by about one percentage point for every 0.01 of reflex. All aerodynamic inputs are engineering estimates; the results are a design-level trade study and not a substitute for wind-tunnel or flight data.

papers.summary: Abstract. Bedrock moisture plays a crucial role in buffering drought, sustaining vegetation, and recharging groundwater in mountainous landscapes with shallow soils. Stronger weathering is generally assumed to enhance these functions by increasing bedrock water availability. However, our understanding of how weathering regulates the storage, retention, and release of rock moisture is still limited. In this study, using two years of high-frequency moisture observations, we quantified relative water storage, temporal stability, and storage-deficit dynamics across the soil–bedrock continuums of two adjacent hillslopes with contrasting weathering intensities in a representative humid karst catchment. Despite having 21% greater maximum dynamic storage capacity than the weakly weathered hillslope (WWH), the strongly weathered hillslope (SWH) realized only 91.65% of the water storage observed at WWH, indicating that greater storage space did not translate into greater realized storage. Strong weathering promoted rapid infiltration and drainage, thereby reducing bedrock water-storage persistence, as indicated by the faster groundwater recession and less persistent shallow groundwater at the SWH. More importantly, these hydrological contrasts also shaped the responses of the two hillslopes to meteorological drought, with the SWH experiencing a greater decline in water storage than the WWH when annual precipitation notably reduced. This greater sensitivity to reduced rainfall may partly explain the shorter trees and smaller stem diameters observed at the SWH. Accordingly, these results challenge the assumption that stronger weathering could increase water availability, providing key insights into drought resilience, groundwater recharge, and runoff generation in karst critical zones.

papers.summary: In the context of climate change, the future precipitation patterns have brought great uncertainty to the drainage systems of mountainous cities, which further exacerbates the risks of urban flooding and non-point source pollution. This study aims to access the impact of projected rainfall on drainage loads and pollutant wash-off dynamics based on three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5) in Qijiang District, Chongqing. The CMCC-ESM2 climate model was combined with the Storm Water Management Model (SWMM) to perform the simulations. Results showed that as the severity of the scenarios set in the scenario simulation increased, both the rainfall intensity and the pollutant load showed a gradual upward trend. Under the SSP5-8.5, for a recurrence period of 100a, the 24h design precipitation increased by 38.65% compared to the historical baseline. In contrast, the increase was more moderate in the SSP1-2.6 and SSP2-4.5 scenarios. Surface runoff exhibited a disproportionate amplification across all scenarios due to infiltration saturation. The 10a runoff magnitude under SSP5-8.5 approximated the historical 50a level. Total pollutant loading showed a stepwise increase across the three pathways, where COD and TSS exhibited greater sensitivity to climate fluctuations than TN and TP. The first flush effect (FF30) strengthened alongside emission intensities, with indices under SSP5-8.5 persistently exceeding the 0.6 strong-effect threshold. This puts a massive strain on existing infrastructure, both hydraulically and environmentally. By elucidating the systematic response of urban catchments to climate change, this research provides a vital scientific basis for informing resilient urban water management in mountainous regions.

papers.title: Soil Salinity in Irrigated Punjab, Pakistan: Drivers, Impacts on Agricultural Productivity, and Integrated Management Strategies
papers.source: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development
papers.summary: Soil salinity and sodicity are major land-degradation challenges affecting the sustainability of irrigated agriculture in Punjab, Pakistan. The region's semi-arid climate, high evaporative demand, dependence on irrigation, variable groundwater quality, inadequate drainage, and long-term salt accumulation create conditions that can impair soil productivity and crop performance. Salinity reduces plant water uptake through osmotic stress and may cause ion toxicity and nutrient imbalances, whereas sodicity deteriorates soil structure, infiltration, and hydraulic conductivity through excessive exchangeable sodium. These problems frequently coexist, complicating the management of salt-affected soils. This review synthesizes research on the major causes, agricultural consequences, and amelioration strategies relevant to Punjab's irrigated farming systems. Particular attention is given to canal–groundwater conjunctive use, irrigation-water quality assessment, drainage and leaching, gypsum application, organic amendments, salt-tolerant crops, improved fertilizer management, and emerging biological approaches. Research conducted in Punjab demonstrates that combining chemical amendments with organic materials and appropriate water management can improve soil conditions and support rice–wheat production on salt-affected land. Nevertheless, the success of reclamation depends on soil texture, salinity and sodicity severity, groundwater depth, water quality, drainage capacity, and farmers' access to inputs and technical advice. The review advocates a site-specific, integrated management framework supported by regular soil and irrigation-water testing, targeted reclamation, salt-tolerant cropping systems, and long-term monitoring. Coordinated action among researchers, extension services, irrigation agencies, and farmers is essential to reduce salt accumulation, restore degraded land, and strengthen agricultural sustainability and food security in Punjab.

This study employed numerical simulations to investigate the impacts of rainfall infiltration on groundwater seepage under the effect of urban construction. A numerical model was established to predict groundwater level (GWL) in the phreatic aquifer (Aq0), incorporating the actual distribution of impervious surfaces and subsurface structures for a representative urban area in Shanghai. The model accounted for land surface conditions through rainfall infiltration coefficients, while subsurface structures were parameterized using equivalent hydraulic conductivity ( K eq ) derived from effective medium theory. Validation results show that the model achieved a maximum error of only 1.7%, demonstrating reliable performance in predicting groundwater seepage. There is 23.23% area with GWL declining more than 0.4 m in the actual scenario with 93% impervious surface hardening comparing without surface hardening. Prediction scenarios with varying reduction rates of impervious surface compared with the actual scenario ( R a ) were conducted to investigate the impact of surface hardening on GWL. The results indicate average GWL of the study area presents exponential decay with the impervious surface ratio. Further, the variations in GWL of Aq0 were investigated by reducing hardened surfaces in different locations with the same R a . As the proportion of underground structures in the reduced impervious surface increases, the area with the same increment of GWL decreases. Prioritizing low impact development in areas with lower subsurface structure density can significantly enhance the efficiency of groundwater recharge by rainfall infiltration.

papers.title: A scenario-based economic valuation framework for ecosystem service benefits of biochar-mediated soil erosion control
papers.summary: Abstract This study quantifies the gross ecosystem-service benefits of biochar-mediated soil erosion control across climate, agricultural, and water-system pathways, while treating runoff reduction as a non-monetised hydrological co-benefit. Soil erosion is a major driver of land degradation, with global losses exceeding billions of tonnes annually and affecting approximately 24% of European land. Meta-analytical evidence indicates that biochar application reduces soil erosion by 16% and surface runoff by 25% on average, with stronger effects observed in erosion-prone environments. Using this evidence, three baseline erosion scenarios were evaluated. Under low, moderate, and high baseline erosion scenarios, central gross benefits were €2.80, €9.33, and €24.19 ha⁻ 1 yr⁻ 1 , respectively. Monte Carlo analysis yielded median total values of €2.95 (95% uncertainty interval: €1.36–€7.48), €9.85 (€4.54–€24.92), and €25.52 (€13.81–€56.21) ha⁻ 1 yr⁻ 1 , respectively. These estimates exclude biochar production, transport, and application costs and therefore represent gross co-benefits rather than net economic returns. Mediterranean experiments reported erosion reductions of up to 67%, substantially above the global mean, illustrating the strong context dependence of biochar responses but not providing a basis for regional economic extrapolation. The results identify soil erosion control as a potentially measurable co-benefit of biochar deployment across climate, agricultural, and water systems. The framework provides a transparent basis for future site- and region-specific valuation while explicitly accounting for uncertainty in biophysical and economic parameters.
