papers.title: Impacts of Cover Crops, No-Tillage and Cotton-Sorghum Rotation on Soil-Water Dynamics: Environmental and Economic Implications
papers.summary: Water scarcity associated with declining groundwater levels in the Ogallala Aquifer threatens the long-term sustainability of irrigated agriculture in the semi-arid Texas High Plains. As irrigation capacity decreases, management strategies that improve soil-mediated water capture and enhance production resilience are increasingly important. This thesis integrates a regional literature synthesis with field-based evaluation of conservation practices aimed at improving water-use efficiency in cotton-based cropping systems. The literature identifies irrigation technology improvements, precision agriculture technologies, and soil health management as key pathways for reducing water demand and enhancing precipitation capture, while also emphasizing economic constraints and site-specific performance of conservation practices. A two-year field study assessed the short-term effects of cover crops and cotton–sorghum rotation under no-tillage on soil physical properties, crop productivity, and economic indicators. Soil measurements included saturated hydraulic conductivity, aggregate stability, compaction, and total organic carbon, alongside cotton and sorghum yield and fiber quality. Results showed limited short-term changes in most soil properties, although aggregate stability increased under rotational systems with cover crops. Cotton yield remained consistent across treatments, but fiber quality and associated economic returns declined in rotation-based systems. Sorghum performance was largely influenced by interannual climatic variability rather than management effects. Overall, findings suggest that while conservation practices hold potential to improve soil function and water-use efficiency, measurable agronomic and economic benefits may require long-term adoption. Extended evaluation is necessary to determine whether gradual soil health improvements can enhance system resilience and profitability under increasing water limitations.

papers.summary: Hydraulic anisotropy in unsaturated soils significantly influences rainfall-induced slope failures, yet limited research has characterized its variation with depth. This study examines the hydraulic anisotropy of a layered unsaturated soil profile from 0.5m to 3.0m depth at 0.5m intervals and quantifies its impact on slope stability under transient infiltration. Laboratory characterization included index properties, Soil-Water Characteristic Curve (SWCC) and saturated permeability measurements for both vertical and horizontal flow directions. Results revealed consistent hydraulic anisotropy (Kr = Kₕ/Kv) ranging from 1.15 to 1.91 across depths, with highest anisotropy near the surface decreasing with depth due to overburden compression. Fines content exhibited a strong inverse relationship with permeability, reaching a minimum of 1.61×10−8 m/s at 1.5m depth where fines peaked at 59%. Numerical modeling using GeoStudio (SEEP/W and SLOPE/W) simulated 12-day rainfall (20 mm/day) followed by 12-day evaporation for 30° and 45° slopes under isotropic and anisotropic conditions. Results demonstrate that anisotropic conditions consistently produced lower factors of safety than isotropic assumptions at the critical Day 12 minimum, with the most pronounced effect observed on the 30° slope with a shallow slip surface, where anisotropy reduced the FoS by approximately 27.3%. For 45° slopes, reductions of 6.6% and 7.3% were recorded for deep-seated and shallow surfaces respectively, while the 30° deep- seated case showed a negligible difference of less than 1.0%. This research highlights that incorporating depth-dependent anisotropic hydraulic properties is essential for accurate rainfall- induced slope failure assessment.

papers.title: Finite Element Method Simulations of Redox Processes in Nanoporous Gold and in Lithium Batteries
papers.source: Carl von Ossiezky University of Oldenburg
papers.summary: This thesis investigates the transport phenomena in nanoporous electrodes and in lithium electrodes using a combination of scanning electrochemical microscopy (SECM) and finite element method (FEM) simulations. The primary goal is to develop and validate analytical models that accurately describe key properties such as porosity, film thickness, and current density distribution in electrochemical systems with complex geometries. Initial studies are devoted to heterogeneous models of nanoporous gold (NPG) and platinum on carbon (Pt/C), highlighting how variations in pore structure impact electrochemical responses. These findings led to the development of improved analytical equations that capture the dynamics of mass transport more effectively. Subsequently, homogeneous models are introduced to simplify the representation of transport by diffusion properties while maintaining accuracy across a range of porosities. A new analytical equation for SECM approach curves was developed, validated through simulations, and shown to be applicable under diverse experimental conditions. The thesis further examines lithium electrodes and SEI evolution using numerical simulations to model the secondary current density distribution under realistic conditions. The results demonstrate how probe positioning and geometry affect the local current density distribution and data interpretation, offering practical guidance for minimizing measurement artefacts in SEI studies. Overall, this work provides valuable tools for optimizing electrode design and contributes to advancing high-performance electrochemical systems.

papers.summary: The influence of climate change on slope stability has become increasingly relevant in recent years, particularly in tropical regions like Malaysia, where the frequency and severity of rainfall events are anticipated to vary considerably. This study examined the combined impacts of rainfall variability and soil desiccation cracking on the slope stability in Malaysia’s tropical granitic residual soils. The study conducted a comprehensive analysis of precipitation patterns utilizing both historical and projected climatic data across multiple climate change scenarios. It subsequently investigated the formation of desiccation cracks in soils exposed to repeated cycles of wetting and drying under controlled laboratory circumstances, replicating actual seasonal variations. Numerical models evaluated the impact of rainfall infiltration on slope stability amid changing climatic circumstances. The rainfall pattern analysis revealed a notable tendency of increasing wet-season rainfall but a considerable decline in dry-season precipitation. papers.title: Identifying strategies to improve the water productivity of permanent raised beds
papers.source: University of Southern Queensland ePrints (University of Southern Queensland)
papers.summary: Permanent raised bed (PRB) farming systems combine several elements (e.g. reduced tillage, controlled traffic, stubble retention) of conservation agriculture. PRB systems have recently been introduced into irrigated areas but there is a lack of information on the agronomic and irrigation performance of these systems under these conditions.
